newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Bedraggled Rwandans emerge from Zaire jungle.
newsitem.headline: Bedraggled Rwandans emerge from Zaire jungle.

text.p: Bedraggled and sick Rwandan refugees emerging from Zaire's jungle behind rebel lines said on Sunday they want to go home and thousands more were on the way.
Hundreds of refugees were found in the wreckage of Tingi Tingi camp, which was abandoned by 170,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees nine days ago shortly before it was overrun by Zairean rebels.

"More are coming in every day and they say there are thousands more coming from the forest. They say they want to go home," Martin Griffiths, U.N. humanitarian coordinator for the Great Lakes region of central Africa, told Reuters at the camp.
"These we see here are in a very poor condition which is one of the determining factors in making them return to the camp."
Griffiths headed representatives of four U.N. agencies and Medecins sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Borders) who flew on Sunday to Tingi Tingi from the rebel-held eastern city of Goma.

It was the first time rebels have allowed aid agencies access to areas near the frontlines to the west. Tingi Tingi is 210 km (130 miles) southeast of the northeastern Zairean capital of Kisangani, a main target for the advancing rebel forces.
The refugees were mostly clustered inside huts built of wooden poles and scraps of plastic sheeting near the camp's main road. All were clearly malnourished and many were also sick.
In a dark corner of a flimsy shelter, a boy who appeared to be around 10 years old sat with his head in his hands, slowly rocking backwards and forwards. Nobody was taking care of him.

At least a dozen other abandoned children wandered the mostly deserted camp, littered with empty ammunition boxes and scraps of military clothing left behind by Hutu former Rwandan soldiers and extremist militiamen who fled with the refugees.

Griffiths said U.N. agencies might within a week be able to airlift out the weakest and would then have to push for permission to use the road to the eastern city of Bukavu on the border with Rwanda and bring in trucks to evacuate the others.
"Because of the level of malnutrition we will bring food for several hundred people," said Abdul Wahab Mahmoud of the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) during the visit to Tingi Tingi.
"The idea is not to create a (new) camp, it is to feed and strengthen the refugees and then repatriate them," he added.

The U.N. refugee agency estimates more than 700 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees have so far returned to the ruins of Tingi Tingi and another 250 have gone back to a makeshift camp at Amisi, seized by rebel forces a week or so earlier.
Many of the refugees who left Tingi Tingi headed west through dense jungle to Ubundu on the Zaire river and towards Kisangani.
WFP said it and the Caritas aid agency started on Saturday distributing food brought to Ubundu town by rail from Kisangani to between 10,000 and 20,000 refugees and Zairean displaced.
Aid workers said they expected more people fleeing the rebel advance to arrive in Ubundu in the next few days. Many children and elderly are malnourished or sick after months on the road.

A U.N. refugee agency spokesman said any mass return of the refugees to Rwanda and Burundi depended on a ceasefire, which on Saturday was ruled out by rebel leader Laurent Kabila who wants President Mobutu Sese Seko first to open talks with him.
Zaire's government on Wednesday accepted a five-point U.N. peace plan, of which the first item is an immediate ceasefire, under pressure from the rebel advances in the east and south.
But the rebels say they will only negotiate with ailing 66-year-old Mobutu and only about his standing down from power.

The president, who is believed to have amassed a personal fortune of billions of dollars in his 31 years of rule over Africa's third largest country, is now staying in the south of France following surgery for prostrate cancer last August.

UNHCR says some 350,000 Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees have plunged deep into the dense jungle of eastern Zaire since fleeing their camps in border areas of the east to escape the rebellion since October spearheaded by ethnic Tutsi Zaireans.
The refugees include Hutu former Rwandan troops and militiamen who led Rwanda's genocide and are fighting alongside Zairean forces in a desperate bid to turn back the rebels.
The refugees and former killers fled Rwanda in 1994 in fear of reprisals for the genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates. Some say they will be killed by the rebels.
